explanation: When they sleep, glass frogs pack nearly all their red blood cells into their liver, which makes their bodies even harder for predators to see.

Poison dart frogs, horned frogs and leopard frogs do not have see-through bellies.
Sleeping glass frogs store nearly all of their red blood cells in the liver, which makes them more transparent.

evidence.summaryExcerpt: The study is "Glassfrogs conceal blood in their liver to maintain transparency," published in *Science* on December 22, 2022 (vol. 378, pp. 1315–1320; DOI 10.1126/science.abl6620), by Carlos Taboada and colleagues. The headline figure is about 89%. The paper's abstract says resting frogs remove roughly 89% of their red blood cells from circulation and pack them into the liver, which raises transparency two- to threefold. Other coverage reports the same numbers: the liver holds about 89% of the cells during rest, and the researchers measured an 80–90% drop in circulating cells.

claimResults.note: The Tier A source, the Science paper (Taboada et al. 2022, DOI 10.1126/science.abl6620), confirms the mechanism and the gain in transparency, but its figure is about 89 per cent, and other coverage reports an 80 to 90 per cent drop in circulating cells. 'Nearly all' overstates nine in ten, so c3 is not confirmed as written.

issues.note: c3 and the explanation say sleeping glass frogs pack 'nearly all' their red blood cells into the liver; the published figure is about 89 per cent (Science, 2022).
